what_its_for: This medicine is used to treat a rare disease called Adenosine Deaminase Severe Combined Immune Deficiency (ADA-SCID). This is a condition where your immune system cannot fight infections properly because your body is missing an important enzyme called ADA. This medicine replaces that missing enzyme to help your immune system work better and protect you from serious infections.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) into the muscle, usually in the thigh or upper arm. It is always given by a doctor, nurse, or trained healthcare provider in a medical setting. You will NOT give this shot to yourself at home. Each injection is given once a week, and your healthcare team will schedule your weekly appointments. Do not skip or delay your injections, as keeping a regular schedule is very important for this medicine to work.
dosing: Your doctor will calculate the right dose specifically for you based on your body weight and your lab test results. The dose may be adjusted over time depending on how your body responds to the medicine. It is very important to attend all lab appointments so your doctor can monitor your levels and make sure you are getting the right amount.
missed_dose: If you miss your weekly injection appointment, contact your doctor or clinic as soon as possible to reschedule. Try to get the missed dose as soon as you can, but do not try to give yourself an extra dose or a double dose to make up for the missed one. Talk to your healthcare team about what to do if appointments are missed repeatedly.
storage: This medicine is stored and handled by your healthcare provider or pharmacy. It must be kept in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). It should NOT be frozen. The vial should be kept in its original carton to protect it from light. Do not use the medicine if it appears cloudy, discolored, or has particles floating in it. If you have any questions about storage, ask your pharmacist or healthcare provider.
what_to_avoid: Avoid skipping your weekly injection appointments, as missing doses can cause your immune system to weaken again and increase your risk of serious infections. Talk to your doctor before getting any vaccines, especially live vaccines (such as measles-mumps-rubella or chickenpox vaccines), as these may not be safe while you are on this medicine. Avoid contact with people who are sick with contagious illnesses, especially while your immune system is still recovering. Always tell all of your doctors and dentists that you are taking this medicine.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: signs of a serious allergic reaction such as hives, rash, swelling of the face or throat, difficulty breathing, dizziness, or rapid heartbeat; signs of infection such as fever, chills, cough, or unusual tiredness; unusual bruising or bleeding; or any new or worsening symptoms. Also call your doctor if you notice pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site that seems severe or gets worse over time.
when_it_works: This medicine begins working to replace the missing ADA enzyme right away, but it may take several weeks to months before your immune system becomes strong enough to fully protect you from infections. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular blood tests to check your enzyme levels and immune cell counts. Be patient and continue attending all of your appointments even if you feel fine, because ongoing treatment is important to keep your immune system working.
special_populations: Children and Infants: This medicine is approved for use in babies, children, and adults. Dosing in children is carefully calculated based on body weight, and children will be monitored closely. Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before starting or continuing this medicine. It is not fully known how this medicine may affect an unborn baby or breast milk. Older Adults: There is limited information about use in older adults. Your doctor will monitor you closely and adjust your dose as needed. Kidney or Liver Problems: Tell your doctor if you have any kidney or liver problems, as this may affect how your body handles the medicine.
